hints: At the maximum point, differentiate $y=(x+5)(3-2x)^{1/2}$ and set $dy/dx=0$.
Use both the product rule and chain rule; factor $(3-2x)^{-1/2}$ from the derivative.
Since the factor is non-zero at the interior maximum, set the remaining linear expression equal to zero to find the exact $x$-coordinate.
Substitute that value into the original curve and simplify the square root to obtain the exact $y$-coordinate.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = (x + 5)\sqrt{3 - 2x} = (x + 5)(3 - 2x)^{1/2}$ using the product rule and chain rule:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = (1)(3 - 2x)^{1/2} + (x + 5)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}(3 - 2x)^{-1/2}(-2)\right)$$
$$= (3 - 2x)^{1/2} - (x + 5)(3 - 2x)^{-1/2}$$

Factor out $(3 - 2x)^{-1/2}$ to simplify the derivative:
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = (3 - 2x)^{-1/2}\left[(3 - 2x) - (x + 5)\right] = (3 - 2x)^{-1/2}(3 - 2x - x - 5) = (3 - 2x)^{-1/2}(-3x - 2)$$

Set the derivative equal to zero to find the stationary point $M$:
$$-3x - 2 = 0 \implies 3x = -2 \implies x = -\dfrac{2}{3}$$

Calculate the exact $y$-coordinate by substituting $x = -\dfrac{2}{3}$ into the curve equation:
$$x + 5 = -\dfrac{2}{3} + 5 = \dfrac{13}{3}$$
$$3 - 2x = 3 - 2\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) = 3 + \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{13}{3}$$
$$y = \left(\dfrac{13}{3}\right)\sqrt{\dfrac{13}{3}} = \dfrac{13\sqrt{13}}{3\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{13\sqrt{39}}{9}$$

ai_rubric.Finding Stationary Points: Applies the product rule to derive $(x+5)p(3-2x)^{-1/2}+q(3-2x)^{1/2}$; Derives a derivative, e.g. $-(x+5)(3-2x)^{-1/2}+(3-2x)^{1/2}$; Concludes with $M\left(-\frac23,\frac{13\sqrt{39}}9\right)$.

skill_tags: Finding an Area Under a Curve

hints: The curve meets the $x$-axis when $x+5=0$ and when $3-2x=0$; use these as the area limits.
Transform both limits: as $x$ runs from $-5$ to $3/2$, $u$ runs from $13$ to $0$.
Integrate the resulting combination of $u^{1/2}$ and $u^{3/2}$, then evaluate exactly and factor out $\sqrt{13}$.
walkthrough:
Determine the limits of integration from the $x$-intercepts of $y = (x + 5)\sqrt{3 - 2x}$ where $y = 0$:
$$(x + 5)\sqrt{3 - 2x} = 0 \implies x = -5 \quad \text{and} \quad x = \dfrac{3}{2}$$

Apply the substitution $u = 3 - 2x$:
$$\mathrm{d}u = -2\,\mathrm{d}x \implies \mathrm{d}x = -\dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u$$
$$2x = 3 - u \implies x = \dfrac{3 - u}{2}$$
$$x + 5 = \dfrac{3 - u}{2} + 5 = \dfrac{13 - u}{2}$$

Convert the limits of integration:
$$\text{At } x = -5: \quad u = 3 - 2(-5) = 3 + 10 = 13$$
$$\text{At } x = \dfrac{3}{2}: \quad u = 3 - 2\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right) = 3 - 3 = 0$$

Substitute into the area integral and invert limits to absorb the negative sign:
$$\text{Area} = \int_{13}^0 \left(\dfrac{13 - u}{2}\right) u^{1/2} \left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{d}u\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}\int_0^{13} (13u^{1/2} - u^{3/2})\,\mathrm{d}u$$

Subtract and multiply by the factor $\dfrac{1}{4}$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{338}{3}\sqrt{13} - \dfrac{338}{5}\sqrt{13}\right) = \dfrac{338\sqrt{13}}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{3} - \dfrac{1}{5}\right) = \dfrac{169\sqrt{13}}{2}\left(\dfrac{2}{15}\right) = \dfrac{169}{15}\sqrt{13}$$

State the exact area in the form $a\sqrt{13}$:
$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{169}{15}\sqrt{13}$$

ai_rubric.Finding an Area Under a Curve: Applies the given substitution and reaches $\frac12\int(\frac{13}{2}-\frac u2)u^{1/2}du$ or equivalent. Identifies $x=-5$ and $x=3/2$, equivalently $u=13,0$. The final result is $\dfrac{169\sqrt{13}}{15}$, so $a=169/15$.
